title: Computer Turns On But No Display
cardText: Diagnose a computer that powers on but shows no image on the screen.
Check monitor power, cables, input source, graphics output, RAM and POST indicators.
Distinguish monitor and connection problems from internal hardware startup faults.
text: This guide is for computers that appear to power on but show no picture.
Begin with the monitor, display cable and video connection before opening the computer.
Check whether the computer shows any startup logo or diagnostic information.
If there is never any video output, investigate POST indicators, graphics hardware and RAM.
Internal hardware checks are intended for people comfortable working inside desktop computers.

confirmPowerActivity.title: Confirm the computer has power activity
body: Press the power button and observe the computer.
Look for power lights, fan movement, keyboard lights or startup sounds.
A spinning fan does not necessarily mean the computer has completed startup.
If there are no signs of power, use the separate computer no-power guide.
If the computer powers on but shows no picture, continue.

link.name: Dell: No Power, No POST, No Boot or No Video
link.description: Explains how to distinguish different computer startup failures.

useNoPowerGuide.title: Use the computer no-power guide
body: The computer shows no signs of powering on.
This is more likely to involve power delivery than a display connection.
Use the Computer Won't Turn On guide to check the power supply, power cable and other startup issues.

checkMonitorPower.title: Check monitor power
body: Confirm the monitor is switched on.
Check its power indicator and press its menu button.
A monitor may enter standby when it receives no video signal.
If the monitor has no power indicator or menu, check its power cable and outlet.

restoreMonitorPower.title: Restore monitor power
body: Check that the monitor's power cable or external adapter is connected securely.
Try a known-working power outlet.
Press the monitor's power button and check for an indicator light or on-screen menu.
If the monitor still has no power, its power supply or internal hardware may be faulty.
Once the monitor powers on, restart this guide.

checkDisplayMessage.title: Check for a monitor message or startup image
body: Watch the monitor while switching the computer on.
A No Signal or No Cable message usually means the monitor is powered but is not receiving a usable video signal.
Check whether the computer manufacturer's logo, BIOS screen or Windows loading screen appears at any point.
If a startup image appears and the display only goes blank when Windows loads, this may be a software or graphics driver issue.
If the monitor remains completely blank, check its built-in controls.

link.name: Dell: Troubleshoot no-video startup problems
link.description: Explains no-video conditions and how to isolate monitor and computer faults.

windowsDisplayIssue.title: Windows or graphics driver issue possible
body: If the computer displays a startup logo or BIOS screen but becomes blank when Windows loads, it is producing video during startup.
Disconnect unnecessary external displays and restart.
If Windows appears to be running, try Windows + Ctrl + Shift + B to reset the graphics driver.
Try Windows recovery or Safe Mode if the problem persists.
Investigate recent graphics driver updates, display settings and Windows startup problems before replacing hardware.
If the computer never displays anything at all, return to the hardware checks in this guide.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows Startup Settings and Safe Mode
link.description: Instructions for accessing Safe Mode when Windows does not start normally.

adjustMonitorSettings.title: Check monitor brightness and controls
body: Press the monitor's physical menu or joystick button.
Check that the on-screen menu appears.
Increase brightness if it is set very low.
Check whether the monitor is in standby or has a power-saving setting.
If the monitor's own menu does not appear, it may be faulty.
If the menu appears, continue checking the video input.

checkInputSource.title: Check monitor input source
body: Open the monitor's on-screen menu.
Select the input matching the video cable connected to the monitor.
Common inputs include HDMI, DisplayPort, DVI and VGA.
Some monitors have multiple HDMI or DisplayPort inputs, so check the exact socket.
Allow several seconds after changing the input.
checkInputSource.alt: Monitor on-screen input selection menu showing HDMI and DisplayPort options
checkInputSource.caption: Use the monitor's menu to select the input matching the connected display cable.

selectCorrectInput.title: Select the correct display input
body: Select the input corresponding to the connected video cable.
Wait for the monitor to detect the computer's signal.
If a picture appears, incorrect input selection was the problem.
If there is still no picture, continue checking the display cable.

checkDisplayCable.title: Check the display cable connection
body: Check both ends of the video cable.
Ensure the cable is firmly connected to the monitor and computer.
Look for damaged connectors, bent pins or loose adapters.
For DisplayPort cables with locking connectors, release the latch before unplugging.
Temporarily remove unnecessary adapters or extension cables.
Reconnect the cable and test the display.

replaceOrReconnectCable.title: Reconnect or replace the display cable
body: Reconnect the display cable securely at both ends.
If the connector or cable is damaged, replace it with a known-working compatible cable.
Avoid using unnecessary display adapters during troubleshooting.
Test again after reconnecting.
If the problem persists, continue checking the computer's display output.

correctDisplayPort.title: Check the display output used on the computer
body: On a desktop with a dedicated graphics card, the monitor should normally connect to a video output on that graphics card.
Motherboard video outputs require support for integrated graphics from the processor and system configuration.
A motherboard HDMI or DisplayPort socket may not work when the processor has no integrated graphics.
If there is no dedicated graphics card, use a supported motherboard video output.
Check the connected port before changing the display cable.

link.name: ASUS: No Power, No Boot or No Display
link.description: Explains integrated graphics, dedicated graphics cards and display output troubleshooting.

moveDisplayCable.title: Connect to the correct graphics output
body: Connect the monitor to the appropriate graphics card or supported motherboard output.
Confirm the monitor is set to the matching input.
Restart the computer if required.
If video appears, the previous output was unavailable or incorrectly selected.
If there is still no display, continue troubleshooting with a known-working cable.

testAnotherCable.title: Test another display cable
body: Use a known-working display cable of the correct type.
Keep the same computer output and monitor input where possible.
Display cables can fail even when they appear undamaged.
If the replacement works, the original cable was likely faulty or incompatible.
If there is still no display, test another monitor.

badCableFound.title: Faulty display cable
body: The monitor works with a known-working replacement cable.
The original cable was likely damaged or incompatible.
Replace it and test the computer again.

testAnotherMonitor.title: Test with another monitor or TV
body: Connect another known-working monitor or TV to the computer.
Use a compatible, known-working cable and select the correct input.
Test the same computer display output where practical.
If another display works, the original monitor or its configuration is likely responsible.
If neither display works, continue investigating the computer.

monitorFault.title: Original monitor fault likely
body: A different monitor works with the same computer and connection.
The original monitor, its settings or its input connection may be faulty.
If possible, test the original monitor with another computer.
Check its on-screen menu and restore default monitor settings if appropriate.
Arrange repair or replacement if it fails with multiple known-working sources.

checkKeyboardResponse.title: Check whether the computer appears responsive
body: Wait for the computer to finish its normal startup period.
Press Caps Lock or Num Lock and watch for its keyboard indicator changing.
Listen for Windows startup sounds or other signs that the operating system has loaded.
Keyboard indicator response is only a clue. Some keyboards do not show a light or may not initialise until later.
A responsive computer may be running without providing video.
A non-responsive keyboard does not by itself prove that the motherboard has failed.

checkGraphicsOutput.title: Check alternative graphics outputs
body: If the graphics card has another compatible video output, test it using a known-working cable.
For systems with supported integrated graphics, a motherboard video output may also be available.
Do not assume motherboard display sockets work with every processor.
Try another suitable video connection and restart the computer.
If the display works on another output, investigate the original output or graphics configuration.

link.name: ASUS: Graphics output and no-display troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for testing dedicated and integrated graphics outputs.

graphicsOutputIssue.title: Graphics output issue identified
body: The display works when using a different graphics output.
The original port, graphics card or display configuration may be responsible.
Inspect the original connector for damage.
Check the supported outputs and graphics settings for the computer.
Use the working output until the original connection can be diagnosed.

reseatGraphicsCard.title: Check and reseat a dedicated graphics card
body: This step applies to desktop computers with a removable dedicated graphics card.
Shut down the computer, switch off the power supply and disconnect the mains cable.
Allow the computer to cool and follow appropriate anti-static precautions.
If you are comfortable working inside the computer, check that the graphics card is fully seated in its PCIe slot.
Check that any required PCIe power connectors are securely attached.
Do not open a power supply or attempt this procedure on a sealed or unfamiliar computer.
Reconnect power and test the display.
If you are not comfortable opening the computer, arrange hardware assistance instead.

link.name: ASUS: Graphics card troubleshooting
link.description: Manufacturer guidance covering graphics card seating, power connections and display faults.

looseGpuFound.title: Loose graphics card connection likely
body: The display returned after checking or reseating the graphics card.
The problem may have been caused by poor PCIe contact or a loose graphics power connector.
Ensure the graphics card is secured correctly.
If the issue returns, investigate the card, motherboard slot and power supply.

checkPostIndicators.title: Check POST diagnostic indicators
body: Observe the computer's diagnostic lights or listen for beep codes during startup.
Some motherboards have LEDs labelled CPU, DRAM, VGA and BOOT.
A light that remains illuminated may indicate the component or startup stage requiring attention.
Diagnostic lights that briefly illuminate in sequence during startup can be normal.
The exact meaning of a light or beep pattern depends on the computer or motherboard model.
A BOOT indicator often relates to the storage or boot device and does not necessarily explain a complete lack of video.
Consult the manufacturer's manual before interpreting the diagnostic code.

link.name: ASUS: Q-LED motherboard diagnostics
link.description: Explains CPU, DRAM, VGA and BOOT diagnostic indicators.

link.name: Dell: No POST diagnostic indicators
link.description: Guidance for interpreting startup beeps and diagnostic lights.

checkPostIndicators.alt: ASUS motherboard diagnostic LED labels showing CPU, DRAM, VGA and BOOT
checkPostIndicators.caption: Some motherboards use diagnostic LEDs to identify the startup stage that has failed.

identifyPostFault.title: Identify the POST fault category
body: Record the diagnostic LED that remains illuminated or the exact beep pattern.
A DRAM indicator can suggest memory installation, compatibility or memory training problems.
A VGA indicator may point to a graphics card, video output or graphics initialisation problem.
A CPU indicator may involve the processor, power connections or motherboard.
BOOT usually indicates a boot-device problem and may occur after video initialisation.
Use the motherboard or computer manual to interpret the indicator correctly.
Choose the RAM path for a DRAM-related indication; otherwise proceed to further hardware diagnostics.

link.name: ASUS: Q-LED diagnostic reference
link.description: Manufacturer-specific information for identifying POST fault categories.

reseatRam.title: Reseat the RAM
body: This step is intended for desktop computers with accessible RAM modules.
Switch off the computer, disconnect mains power and follow anti-static precautions.
Refer to the motherboard manual before removing any memory.
Release the memory-slot clips and carefully remove the RAM module.
Check the module and slot for obvious contamination or damage.
Align the notch correctly and reinstall the module until it is fully seated and the retaining clips are secure.
Do not force the RAM into the slot.
Reconnect power and allow the computer time to initialise the memory, especially on DDR5 systems.
If the display returns, the problem may have been poor memory contact.
For laptops or sealed systems, follow the manufacturer's service instructions or arrange professional assistance.

link.name: ASUS: No-display memory troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for checking memory installation when the computer does not display.

reseatRam.alt: Desktop RAM module being aligned with a motherboard memory slot
reseatRam.caption: Align the RAM notch with the slot and ensure the module is fully seated.

looseRamFound.title: Loose RAM connection likely
body: The display returned after reseating the memory.
A loose module or poor contact may have prevented the computer from completing POST.
Ensure the memory is fully seated and secured.
If the issue returns, check memory compatibility and run a memory diagnostic when the computer can start.

testSingleRamStick.title: Test one RAM module at a time
body: If the desktop has multiple removable memory modules, test with one module installed at a time.
Switch off and disconnect mains power before changing modules.
Use the single-module slot recommended by the motherboard manual.
Test each module individually in the recommended slot.
If only one module works, test the other module in the same slot to help identify a faulty stick.
If neither module works in one slot, testing a different supported slot may help identify a slot or motherboard problem.
Allow additional time for memory training after each change, particularly on DDR5 systems.
A successful test with one module does not automatically prove the other module is faulty.

link.name: ASUS: Motherboard memory troubleshooting
link.description: Official instructions for testing RAM configurations during no-display troubleshooting.

ramFaultFound.title: RAM module, slot or configuration fault possible
body: The computer displays correctly with one memory configuration but fails with another.
Possible causes include a faulty RAM module, damaged slot, incompatible memory or unstable memory settings.
Test modules individually using the same known-working slot where possible.
Check the motherboard's supported memory configurations.
Replace a module only after further tests confirm it is defective.
If the fault follows a particular memory slot, further motherboard diagnostics may be needed.

clearCmos.title: Reset BIOS or CMOS settings
body: Incorrect firmware settings, memory overclocking or display configuration may prevent the computer from starting correctly.
Record important BIOS settings before making changes if they are known.
A CMOS reset may remove custom boot, storage, memory and security settings.
It may also trigger a BitLocker recovery-key request on some Windows systems after firmware-related changes.
Use the exact motherboard or computer manual for the approved CMOS reset procedure.
Do not move jumpers, remove batteries or open a sealed computer without the correct service instructions.
After the reset, restore any required settings and allow the system time to complete startup.
If you are unsure about the consequences, arrange further diagnostics instead.

link.name: ASUS: No-display troubleshooting and CMOS reset
link.description: Official guidance for resetting firmware settings during startup troubleshooting.

biosSettingsFault.title: BIOS settings fault likely
body: The display returned after resetting firmware settings.
An unstable memory, graphics or overclocking setting may have prevented startup.
Avoid restoring the previous settings without checking their compatibility.
Review any required boot or storage settings before restarting Windows.
If the problem returns, investigate firmware compatibility and motherboard hardware.

hardwareDiagnosticRequired.title: Internal hardware diagnostics required
body: The computer still has no display after checking the monitor, video connection and relevant startup hardware.
Possible causes include graphics card, motherboard, RAM, processor or power supply faults.
Fans and power lights alone do not confirm that the power supply is functioning correctly.
Use manufacturer diagnostic codes and known-working compatible components to isolate the fault.
Check the graphics card power connectors and motherboard power connections where appropriate.
Do not open or attempt to repair the internal components of a power supply.
For laptops, all-in-one computers or sealed systems, follow manufacturer service procedures.
Record diagnostic LED or beep codes and the troubleshooting steps performed before arranging repair.
